t: Lesson 2, Context Files.
Your instructor is Patrick Diamitani.
This is the single biggest upgrade most people never make.
Every new session starts with a blank memory, so you end up explaining your stack, your style,
and your rules again and again.
A context file fixes that.
You write it once, and the agent reads it first every time.
Here's a real one.
It's just a markdown file in your project.
A line about the stack, things to always do, like running the tests, and things to never
do, like committing secrets.
Four things belong in it, your stack and the commands to build and test.
You're always and never rules.
We're the important things live, and how the agent should check its own work.
Every harness reads a file like this, only the name changes.
This .md is the closest thing to a shared standard, and many tools read it.
Write it once and point the others at it.
A few tips.
Keep it short under 200 lines.
Write rules, not essays.
And every time the agent gets something wrong, add a line, so it never happens again.
Quick recap.
A context file is read first, every session, so you never repeat yourself.
For mission, create a clod.
MD with your stack, three always rules and three never rules.
Now your agent remembers.
